docs.title: Welcome to ROXAS AI
docs.text:
ROXAS AI is an open-source, Python-based tool designed to streamline quantitative wood anatomy (QWA) and dendrochronology research. Built as an extensible plugin for the napari multi-dimensional image viewer, it enables researchers to efficiently extract anatomical traits and establish high-resolution time series of cell measurements within dated tree rings.

Currently optimized for linear conifer anatomies (with linear angiosperm anatomies currently in development), ROXAS AI provides an end-to-end workflow—from automated image segmentation to visual cross-dating—on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

docs.title: Why ROXAS AI?
docs.text:
ROXAS AI was developed to modernize and expand upon the foundations of the classical ROXAS implementation. It addresses key limitations of classical workflows to make wood anatomy more accessible, automated, and scalable:

  • Cross-Platform Accessibility

    Runs natively on Windows, macOS, and Linux, bringing quantitative wood anatomy to all operating systems.

  • Open Science & Powerful Viewing

    Built on the open-source napari image viewer, completely eliminating dependencies on proprietary commercial software (such as Image-Pro Plus).

  • Modern AI Segmentation

    Leverages specialized deep-learning neural networks to segment cell lumens and ring boundaries with high accuracy and minimal manual editing.

  • Intuitive End-to-End Workflow

    Combines batch preparation, interactive raster/vector curation, visual cross-dating, and trait extraction into a streamlined, user-friendly interface.

docs.title: High-Level Workflow
docs.text:
ROXAS AI guides you through an end-to-end pipeline from raw wood cross-section images to structured anatomical datasets:

flowchart TD
    A["<b>1. Prepare Images</b><br/>Standardize files & metadata"] --> B["<b>2. AI Segmentation</b><br/>Detect cells & ring boundaries"]
    B --> C["<b>3. Interactive Curation</b><br/>Review & cross-date rings"]
    C --> D["<b>4. Trait Measurement</b><br/>Export CSV tables & plots"]

docs.title: Installation & Setup Guide
docs.text: Welcome to ROXAS AI! This guide walks you through setting up a clean Python environment, installing the napari-roxas-ai plugin, and configuring optional hardware GPU acceleration for fast deep-learning inference.

docs.title: Step 1: Install a Package Manager & Open Terminal
docs.text:
We strongly recommend installing Miniforge (community-driven, pre-configured with the fast conda-forge channel) or Miniconda to manage your Python environment.

WindowsmacOSLinux
  1. Download the installer:
    • Miniforge (Recommended): Download the Miniforge Windows 64-bit Installer.
    • Miniconda (Alternative): Download the Miniconda Windows 64-bit Installer.
  2. Run the installer: Follow the standard setup wizard. We recommend installing for "Just Me" into the default directory.
  3. Open the prompt:
    • Open the Windows Start menu and search for Miniforge Prompt (or Anaconda Prompt if using Miniconda).
    • Alternatively, if you use Windows Terminal or PowerShell and initialized Conda, open your standard terminal.
    • Run all subsequent installation commands inside this prompt.
  1. Download the installer:
    • Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4): Download Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.pkg or the Miniconda Apple Silicon Installer.
    • Intel Macs: Download Miniforge3-MacOSX-x86_64.pkg or the Miniconda Intel Installer.
  2. Run the installer package and follow the prompts.
  3. Alternative (Command-line installation via Terminal): 
    curl -L -O "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-MacOSX-$(uname -m).sh"
bash Miniforge3-MacOSX-$(uname -m).sh
  4. Open Terminal: Open Applications > Utilities > Terminal.
  1. Download and run the installer in Terminal:
    • x86_64 (64-bit Intel/AMD): 
      wget https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
bash Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
    • ARM64 / aarch64: 
      wget https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-aarch64.sh
bash Miniforge3-Linux-aarch64.sh
  2. Follow the installer prompts and answer yes when asked to initialize Conda for your shell.
  3. Close and reopen your Terminal window to activate Conda.

docs.title: Step 2: Create & Activate the Environment
docs.text:
Create a dedicated, clean Python 3.12 environment named roxas-ai and activate it:

conda create -n roxas-ai python=3.12 -y
conda activate roxas-ai

Always activate your environment

Whenever you open a new terminal session to run ROXAS AI, make sure to activate the environment first: 

conda activate roxas-ai

docs.title: Step 3: (Optional) GPU Acceleration
docs.text:
While ROXAS AI functions fully on CPU, enabling GPU acceleration significantly speeds up deep-learning instance segmentation for wood anatomical cells and tree ring boundaries on large, high-resolution scans.

Windows & Linux (NVIDIA GPUs)Windows & Linux (Intel GPUs)macOS (Apple Silicon & Intel)

By default, standard PyPI wheels install a CPU-only build of PyTorch on Windows and Linux. To leverage your NVIDIA GPU:

  1. Install CUDA-enabled PyTorch: 

    pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
    This command installs PyTorch with CUDA 12.8 runtime support, fully compatible with modern NVIDIA GPUs (RTX 20-, 30-, 40-, and 50-series / Blackwell, Ada Lovelace, Ampere, and Turing architectures). The CUDA runtime is bundled with the PyTorch wheels; you only need an up-to-date NVIDIA display driver installed.

    (Note: If your system uses older NVIDIA drivers that cannot be updated, install the CUDA 12.6 build instead by replacing cu128 with cu126).

  2. Verify GPU / CUDA availability: 

    python -c "import torch; print('CUDA available:', torch.cuda.is_available()); print('CUDA version:', torch.version.cuda); print('GPU:', torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'None')"
    For a functional GPU installation, CUDA available: should output True and list your NVIDIA GPU model name.

  3. Troubleshooting: If CUDA available: reports False after installation (e.g., if a CPU-only PyTorch build was previously cached or installed), cleanly remove PyTorch and reinstall with the explicit CUDA wheel index: 

    pip uninstall torch torchvision torchaudio -y
pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

(For supported AMD GPUs on Linux, consult the PyTorch ROCm installation guide).

Experimental

Intel GPU (XPU) acceleration in PyTorch is supported for Intel Arc A-Series and B-Series dedicated graphics cards, as well as Intel Core Ultra processors with integrated Arc graphics on Windows 11 and Ubuntu. See the PyTorch Intel GPU guide for detailed device support.

  1. Install the Intel GPU driver: Download and install the latest graphics driver from Intel's website. No separate oneAPI base toolkit installation is required.

  2. Install XPU-enabled PyTorch: 

    pip install "torch>=2.5,<2.9" "torchvision<0.24" --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu
    The version constraints ensure PyTorch remains within the range supported by ROXAS AI, preventing subsequent pip commands from replacing it with a CPU build.

  3. Verify XPU availability: 

    python -c "import torch; print('XPU available:', getattr(torch, 'xpu', None) is not None and torch.xpu.is_available()); print('GPU:', torch.xpu.get_device_name(0) if getattr(torch, 'xpu', None) and torch.xpu.is_available() else 'None')"
    For a functional installation, XPU available: should output True and list your Intel GPU device name.

First run kernel compilation

On some Intel GPUs, the initial inference pass compiles GPU compute kernels, which can take several minutes with no terminal output. The compiled kernels are cached on disk, so subsequent runs start within seconds.

  • Apple Silicon (M1 / M2 / M3 / M4): PyTorch leverages Apple's Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) backend natively. No additional CUDA or driver configuration is required. The standard PyTorch wheels installed with ROXAS AI automatically include MPS support.

To verify MPS availability in Terminal: 

python -c "import torch; print('MPS available:', torch.backends.mps.is_available()); print('MPS built:', torch.backends.mps.is_built())"
When MPS available: True is displayed, ROXAS AI automatically accelerates deep-learning segmentation using your Apple Silicon GPU.

  • Intel-based Macs: GPU acceleration is not supported on Intel Macs; ROXAS AI will run automatically using the CPU.

docs.text:

pip install --upgrade napari-roxas-ai

docs.title: 1. Launch napari with ROXAS AI
docs.text:
Run the dedicated launcher command in your terminal:

napari-roxas

Why use napari-roxas?

  • Instant Shortcuts: Installs all custom ROXAS AI keyboard and canvas navigation shortcuts (W, A, S, D, Space, and nudging hotkeys) immediately upon startup.
  • Auto-docked Workflow: Opens and docks the Group - Manual Editing widget panel on the right sidebar, ready for immediate use.
  • Duplicate Prevention: Manages dock widgets through the manifest to prevent accidental duplicate panels.

(Note: Starting with plain napari works as well; plugin shortcuts and widgets become active as soon as you open any ROXAS AI widget via Plugins > ROXAS AI).

ROXAS AI workbench initialized in napari with the Manual Editing Group docked in the right sidebar.

docs.title: 2. Verify with Bundled Sample Data
docs.text:
1. In the napari menu, navigate to File > Open Sample > ROXAS AI.
  2. The sample scan and its associated annotation layers will load into the viewer:
    • conifer_sample (Image layer): The raw high-resolution wood cross-section scan.
    • conifer_sample.cells (Labels layer): Labeled individual cell lumen instances.
    • conifer_sample.rings (Labels layer): Labeled annual tree-ring boundaries and ring bands.
    • Rings Years (Points layer): Calendar year text labels dynamically positioned along each ring boundary.

Automatic Background Model & Asset Downloads

Pre-trained deep learning neural network weights (.pth files) and sample image assets are automatically downloaded from remote repositories in the background upon first access and cached locally in your user data directory for all subsequent sessions. Download progress is logged in the terminal.

docs.title: 3. Verify Hardware Acceleration in Settings
docs.text:
1. In napari, open Plugins > ROXAS AI > ZZ - Settings (or click the floating settings icon ⚙️ in the measurement widgets).
  2. Expand the processing section.
  3. Confirm that try_to_use_gpu and try_to_use_autocast are enabled (true).
  4. Click Apply.
  5. Settings apply immediately across all open widgets without requiring a napari restart.

docs.title: Summary Checklist
docs.text:
• [x] Miniforge / Miniconda installed and prompt opened.
  • [x] Dedicated Python 3.12 environment created and activated (conda activate roxas-ai).
  • [x] (Optional) GPU PyTorch installed and tested (CUDA available: True, MPS available: True, or XPU available: True).
  • [x] napari-roxas-ai installed via pip install napari-roxas-ai.
  • [x] Launched using napari-roxas and loaded bundled sample data (File > Open Sample > ROXAS AI).
  • [x] Verified try_to_use_gpu in Plugins > ROXAS AI > ZZ - Settings.

Important note on package installation

Never install or upgrade packages into the environment while napari or any Python script is actively running in it. Always close napari and execute package commands from a dedicated terminal prompt.

docs.title: 1. PyTorch Uses CPU Despite Having an NVIDIA GPU
docs.text:
If PyTorch reports CUDA available: False or runs segmentation on CPU despite an NVIDIA GPU being present: 1. Ensure your NVIDIA graphics card driver is up to date via NVIDIA GeForce Experience or the NVIDIA Driver Downloads page. 2. Check if a CPU-only wheel of PyTorch was installed by another dependency. Reinstall the CUDA 12.8 wheel: 

pip uninstall torch torchvision torchaudio -y
pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128

docs.title: 2. Settings Not Updating or Corrupted Configuration
docs.text:
When upgrading napari-roxas-ai over an older installation, your customized settings.json file is preserved on disk to prevent overwriting user preferences. If you experience unexpected parameter behavior or schema mismatches:

  • Reset via UI: In napari, open Plugins > ROXAS AI > ZZ - Settings and click Reset to defaults.
  • Manual Reset: Delete your local settings file to let ROXAS AI regenerate default settings on next launch:
    • Windows: %LOCALAPPDATA%\napari-roxas-ai\settings.json
    • macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/napari-roxas-ai/settings.json
    • Linux: ~/.config/napari-roxas-ai/settings.json

docs.title: 3. Linux GUI / Wayland Display Issues
docs.text:
On certain Linux distributions using Wayland display servers, Qt6 / napari may encounter rendering glitches or fail to start. If this occurs, force Qt to use X11/XCB: 

export QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb
napari-roxas

docs.title: 4. Complete Clean Reinstallation
docs.text:
If you need to perform a completely fresh reinstallation: 1. Close napari and open your terminal with conda activate roxas-ai. 2. Uninstall the plugin: 

pip uninstall napari-roxas-ai -y
3. Reinstall the latest release: 
pip install napari-roxas-ai
4. Or recreate the entire Conda environment from scratch: 
conda deactivate
conda env remove -n roxas-ai -y
conda create -n roxas-ai python=3.12 -y
conda activate roxas-ai
pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128  # Optional GPU
pip install napari-roxas-ai

docs.title: Deep-Learning Segmentation Models
docs.text: Technical reference on the deep-learning neural network architectures, boundary regression formulation, tiled inference pipeline, and model checkpoint management in ROXAS AI.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Traditional quantitative wood anatomy (QWA) workflows often rely on manual thresholding and morphological filtering, which can be sensitive to staining variations, compression wood, cutting artifacts, or resin deposits. ROXAS AI replaces these manual thresholds with specialized deep-learning models trained specifically on conifer wood micro-sections and surface scans:

  1. Cell Lumina Semantic Segmentation (linear_cells_model): Delineates tracheid cell lumina across whole-slide cross-sections.
  2. Tree-Ring Boundary Regression (linear_rings_model.pth / LinearRingModel_v3_iterative.pt): Detects annual growth boundaries using an iterative regression formulation along the radial axis.

All models run locally on your system using PyTorch and PyTorch Lightning. Inference seamlessly leverages hardware acceleration (NVIDIA CUDA or Apple Silicon Metal Performance Shaders / MPS) when available, falling back to multi-core CPU execution.

docs.title: Cell Segmentation Model
docs.text:
The cell segmentation model automates the detection and lumen delineation of individual tracheids in high-resolution conifer cross-sections.

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           CELL INFERENCE PIPELINE                           |
|                                                                             |
|  [ Full Scan Image ]                                                        |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ Reflection Padding (112 px) ]                                            |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ Tiled Patches: 1024x1024 px, Stride: 800 px ]                            |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ ResNet-50 Encoder + U-Net Decoder (smp.Unet) ]                           |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ Argmax / Binary Class Probability Map ]                                  |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ Center Patch Stitching (800x800 px unpadded region) ]                    |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ Connected-Component Labeling + Border Component Removal ]                |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ Final Binary Mask / Cell Labels Layer (.cells) ]                         |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: Architecture & Parameters
docs.text:
• Architecture: U-Net semantic segmentation network built with a ResNet-50 encoder backbone (initialized via segmentation_models_pytorch).
  • Input Channels & Normalization: Standard 3-channel RGB image patches normalized via ResNet-50 pre-processing statistics.
  • Output Classes: Binary classification (Background vs. Cell Lumen).
  • Inference Mode: Evaluated in eval() mode with automatic mixed precision (torch.autocast) when GPU acceleration is active.

docs.title: Tiled Patch Inference & Reflection Padding
docs.text:
High-resolution anatomical scans frequently exceed tens of thousands of pixels in height and width. To handle massive images with bounded GPU memory usage while preventing edge artifacts:

  1. Patch Dimensions: Patches of dimension \(1024 \times 1024\text{ px}\) are extracted with a sliding stride of \(800\text{ px}\).
  2. Reflection Padding: The full image is padded in reflect mode with a margin of: $\(\text{pad\_size} = \frac{\text{patch\_size} - \text{stride}}{2} = \frac{1024 - 800}{2} = 112\text{ px}\)$
  3. Margin Discarding & Seamless Stitching: Predictions generated on the \(1024 \times 1024\text{ px}\) patch are sliced to retain only the central \(800 \times 800\text{ px}\) region, completely discarding boundary distortion zones before stitching into the final canvas.
  4. Border Component Post-Processing: Cells touching the outer edges of the entire image canvas are filtered out (remove_border_touching_components) to prevent partial, truncated cell measurements.
  5. Instance Labeling: Binary predictions are labeled into discrete cell instances using connected components (skimage.measure.label).

docs.title: Tree-Ring Boundary Segmentation Model
docs.text:
Annual ring boundaries define the temporal framework for dendrochronological dating and ring-width series extraction.

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           RING INFERENCE PIPELINE                           |
|                                                                             |
|  [ Full Scan Image / Radial Microsection ]                                  |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ Iterative Boundary Regression Network (PackageImporter) ]                 |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ Sequential Boundary Polylines (Bark -> Pith) ]                           |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ Coordinate Reordering (Left-to-Right) ]                                  |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ Horizontal Completion to Canvas Margins (x=0 to x=Width) ]                |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ Top Incomplete Boundary Prepended (Dummy Row 0) ]                         |
|         │                                                                   |
|         ▼                                                                   |
|  [ Annual Ring Polygon Bands & Raster Labels (.rings) ]                     |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: Iterative Boundary Regression Formulation
docs.text:
Unlike conventional semantic segmentation models that classify pixels independently (often leading to broken, fragmented, or bleeding ring lines), ROXAS AI adopts an iterative regression formulation:

  • Continuous Coordinate Trajectories: The model regresses ordered coordinate trajectories \(P_k = \{(y_1, x_1), (y_2, x_2), \dots, (y_n, x_n)\}\) representing each annual boundary line sequentially from the bark toward the pith.
  • Topological Continuity: Because boundaries are represented as parametric curves, lines remain unbroken across faint latewood zones, narrow rings, or local staining blemishes.
  • Linear Conifer Adaptation: While the generalized framework supports multi-species circular geometries (Katzenmaier et al. 2025), the integrated model checkpoint is optimized for linear radial microsections common in microtome-based quantitative wood anatomy.

docs.title: Post-Processing & Geometry Construction
docs.text:
Once boundary polyline trajectories are predicted:

  1. Left-to-Right Sorting: Boundary point sequences are sorted from the left margin to the right margin (rearrange_coordinates).
  2. Horizontal Completion: Boundary endpoints are extended horizontally to the image boundaries (\(x = 0\) and \(x = W - 1\)) using horizontal_rings_completion, ensuring complete division into annual polygons without self-intersections.
  3. Dummy Top Boundary: A horizontal reference line is prepended at \(y = 0\) (row index 0) to mark the outer, incomplete growth ring (assigned enabled = False).
  4. Rasterization & Ring Colormap: The enclosed polygonal areas between consecutive boundaries are rasterized into integer labels, rendered using a high-contrast categorical ring colormap.

docs.title: Targeted Re-Segmentation Below a Given Year
docs.text: In the Edit Rings widget (6 - Edit rings), users can re-run the deep-learning model starting from any selected calendar year. The model re-segments all boundaries below that anchor year while preserving manually validated boundaries above it, eliminating the need to re-process the entire image when correcting early-stage errors.

docs.title: Model Weights & Automatic Management
docs.text:
ROXAS AI automatically handles model checkpoint discovery, remote downloads, integrity checks, and local caching.

Model Identifier File Name Format Primary Task Cell Segmentation linear_cells_model.pth PyTorch State Dict / TorchScript Tracheid lumen semantic segmentation Ring Segmentation linear_rings_model.pth PyTorch Package (torch.package) Initial annual ring boundary regression Ring Re-run Model LinearRingModel_v3_iterative.pt PyTorch Package (torch.package) Iterative boundary regression below edited ring

docs.title: Background Download & Local Checkpoints
docs.text:
• Automatic Asset Detection: Upon opening segmentation widgets or running batch inference, ROXAS AI checks local directories (_models/_cells and _models/_rings).
  • GitHub Release Storage: If checkpoints are missing or incomplete, the asset manager (check_assets_and_download) fetches cells_models.zip and rings_models.zip directly from official GitHub releases.
  • Atomic Extraction & Tracking: Archives are downloaded into temporary directories and extracted atomically. A .asset_id marker tracks the release version to prevent duplicate downloads.
  • Offline Reliability: Once downloaded, model checkpoints reside locally and do not require active internet access.

docs.title: Hardware Acceleration & Resource Management
docs.text:
• Device Selection: Controlled via the processing.try_to_use_gpu setting in ZZ - Settings.
  • NVIDIA GPUs: Leverages CUDA acceleration with tensor cores and mixed precision.
  • Apple Silicon: Uses Metal Performance Shaders (mps) backend on M-series chips.
  • CPU Fallback: Seamless fallback on systems without dedicated GPU hardware.
  • Thread Safety: Multithreaded execution sets torch.set_num_threads(1) within background worker threads to prevent OpenMP runtime conflicts across Qt event loops.

docs.title: Keyboard & Mouse Shortcuts Reference
docs.text:
Complete reference of keyboard shortcuts and mouse bindings available in ROXAS AI for high-throughput image navigation, manual vector/raster curation, and workflow dock management in napari.

Shortcut Availability & Activation

  • Launching via napari-roxas: Running the custom launcher napari-roxas installs all navigation and workflow shortcuts immediately upon startup and opens the Manual Editing dock container.
  • Launching via standard napari: When starting via plain napari, shortcuts and duplicate dock protection are installed and activated as soon as any ROXAS AI widget or menu action is opened.

docs.title: 1. Viewport Navigation & Magnification
docs.text:
Wood anatomical cross-sections can contain millions of pixels. Single-key navigation shortcuts allow rapid, continuous inspection without switching between active drawing/selection tools:

  • Single-Key Panning (W/A/S/D or Arrow Keys): Shifts the visible camera viewport by 200 screen pixels in the corresponding direction.
  • Fast Panning (Shift + Navigation Keys): Doubles the movement step to 400 screen pixels, useful for traversing long radial stem increments.
  • Incremental Zoom (Q / E): Adjusts camera magnification by \(\pm 0.25\) zoom increments while keeping the viewport centered.

docs.title: 2. Workflow Dock Groups & Sidebar Management
docs.text:
ROXAS AI organizes its 11 tools into unified, scrollable dock containers to keep the workspace clean:

  • Manual Editing Group (Ctrl + Shift + M / macOS: Cmd + Shift + M): Opens the primary interactive analysis workflow containing 2/4 - Load image(s), 3A - Detect cells & rings, 5 - Edit cells, 6 - Edit rings, and 9A - Measure cells & rings.
  • Batch Operations Group (Ctrl + Shift + B / macOS: Cmd + Shift + B): Opens the high-throughput batch pipeline containing 1 - Prepare project images, 3B - Batch detect cells & rings, and 9B - Batch measure & update.
  • Close All Docks (Ctrl + Shift + W / macOS: Cmd + Shift + W): Clears all open dock widgets to maximize screen real estate for visual inspection.

docs.title: 3. Cell Editing Shortcuts (5 - Edit cells)
docs.text:
In the Edit Cells widget, shortcuts streamline both pixel-level raster touch-ups and vector polygon curation:

  • Dynamic Brush Resizing (Ctrl + Mouse Wheel / macOS: Cmd + Wheel):
  • While using the Paint Brush or Eraser in Raster mode, holding Ctrl and scrolling dynamically adjusts brush diameter between 1 and 100 pixels.
  • Step scaling is proportional: \(\text{step} = \max(1.0, 0.15 \times \text{brush\_size})\), providing single-pixel precision at small diameters and rapid scaling at large sizes.
  • Standard napari dimension slider scrolling is temporarily suppressed during editing to prevent accidental slice jumps.
  • Brush / Eraser Quick Toggle (Ctrl + Double-Click / macOS: Cmd + Double-Click):
  • Holding Ctrl and double-clicking on the canvas instantly swaps between painting and erasing modes without needing to click toolbar icons.
  • Lasso & Shape Polygon Deletion (Delete or Backspace):
  • In Vector mode with Lasso Select active, drawing one or more closed loops and pressing Delete removes all cell polygons that intersect the lasso selection. Selecting cell polygons directly with the shape selection tool and pressing Delete also deletes the selected cells.
  • Undo Stack (Ctrl + Z / macOS: Cmd + Z):
  • Maintains a history of up to 50 operations. In vector mode, it restores exact shape geometries and properties; in raster mode, it triggers napari's label brush undo history.

docs.title: 4. Tree-Ring Editing Shortcuts (6 - Edit rings)
docs.text:
In the Edit Rings widget, shortcuts facilitate precise alignment of vector polylines:

  • Fine Boundary Nudging (1 px):
  • Select one or more boundary polylines using the Direct Select tool and press Ctrl + ↑ / ↓ / ← / → (or Cmd + Arrows on macOS).
  • Shifts all vertices of selected boundaries by exactly 1 pixel, ideal for sub-lumen alignment along latewood cell walls.
  • Fast Boundary Nudging (10 px):
  • Press Ctrl + Shift + Arrow keys to shift selected boundary vertices by 10 pixels per step.
  • Topmost Lasso Vertex Deletion (Delete or Backspace):
  • When Lasso Select is active in ring editing mode, drawing a selection loop and pressing Delete removes vertices located inside the lasso.
  • Topmost Layer Priority Rule: When multiple boundary polylines overlap closely within the lasso area, vertices are removed exclusively from the topmost boundary (highest shape index), preventing accidental deletion of underlying ring lines.
  • Undo History (Ctrl + Z / macOS: Cmd + Z):
  • Restores prior boundary polylines, calendar year metadata assignments, deleted vertex markers, and affine transform modifications across a 50-step history stack.

docs.title: Image Orientation & Coordinate Conventions
docs.text: Linear input images have to be oriented with +/- horizontal rings and the bark side at the bottom. In napari and exported tables, coordinates use row-major (y, x) pixel coordinates (origin (0, 0) at the top-left), where row index y increases downward towards the bark and column index x increases from left to right across the radial section.

docs.title: File Formats
docs.text: ROXAS AI uses a standardized naming convention to organize analysis data. For a sample named sample_01, the following files are typically generated:

docs.title: Spatial & Image Files
docs.text:
• .scan.jpg / .scan.tif etc.: The original high-resolution scan of the wood sample; supported image formats: JPG, JPEG, TIFF, TIF, PNG, BMP, JP2.
  • .cells.png: A label image produced by the deep-learning cell segmentation model (Segmentation Models) where each pixel value corresponds to a unique cell ID (CID).
  • .rings.tif: A label image (or vector-like representation) produced by the deep-learning ring boundary segmentation model (Segmentation Models) containing the identified tree-ring boundaries.
  • _annotated.jpg: A visualization of the scan with ring boundaries and year labels overlaid for quick review. This file is automatically generated after segmentation (3A/3B), after updating the outermost ring year (6), after applying a cross-dating offset (7) and with every measurement (9A/9B). Manual saves (Save All Layers) do not redraw it.
  • _ReferenceSeries.jpg: (Optional) A visual representation of the reference chronologies used during cross-dating.

docs.title: Data & Metadata Files
docs.text:
• .metadata.json: A comprehensive JSON file containing sample information, imaging parameters, and all processing thresholds required to reproduce the analysis.
  • .cwt.json: A JSON file storing cell wall thickness (CWT) quality assurance circles, centroid coordinates, thickness values, inclusion/exclusion status, and filter reasons for sampled cells. It is created during trait measurement (9A/9B) and automatically loaded into napari as the [<sample>] CWT Circles Shapes layer when reopening samples.
  • .cells_table.csv: A CSV file (semicolon-delimited by default, configurable in settings) containing measurements for every individual cell.
  • .rings_table.csv: A CSV file (semicolon-delimited by default, configurable in settings) containing aggregated measurements for each tree ring.

docs.title: Theoretical Hydraulic Conductance (KH)
docs.text:
Theoretical hydraulic conductance is approximated using Poiseuille's law adjusted for elliptical tubes (Nonweiler 1975):

\[ \text{KH} = \frac{\text{LA}_{\text{m}^2} \cdot m^2}{\nu \cdot k} \]

Where:

  • \(\text{LA}_{\text{m}^2}\): Cell lumen area converted to square meters (\(\text{LA}_{\text{m}^2} = \text{LA} \cdot 10^{-12}\,\text{m}^2\)).
  • \(m\): Mean hydraulic radius defined as lumen area divided by ellipse circumference (\(m = \text{LA}_{\text{m}^2} / C\), in meters). The circumference \(C\) is computed using Ramanujan's formula: \(C \approx \pi \left[ 3(a + b) - \sqrt{(3a + b)(a + 3b)} \right]\), where \(a = \sqrt{\text{ASP} \cdot \text{LA}_{\text{m}^2} / \pi}\) is the semi-major axis and \(b = \text{LA}_{\text{m}^2} / (\pi a)\) is the semi-minor axis in meters.
  • \(k\): Geometric form factor for elliptical cross-sections (Nonweiler 1975): \(k = \frac{4}{1 + \sqrt{1 - e^4}}\), where \(e = \sqrt{\frac{a^2 - b^2}{a^2}}\) is the elliptical eccentricity (\(e \in [0, 1)\)).
  • \(\nu\): Dynamic viscosity of water at 20°C (\(1.002 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{MPa}\cdot\text{s}\), equivalent to \(1.002 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\text{Pa}\cdot\text{s}\)).

For ring-level summaries, KH is calculated as the sum of all individual cell conductances in that annual ring:

\[ \text{KH}_{\text{ring}} = \sum_{i=1}^{\text{CNO}} \text{KH}_i \]

docs.title: Specific Hydraulic Conductivity (KS)
docs.text:
Specific hydraulic conductivity normalizes the ring's theoretical conductance by the total cross-sectional ring area RA (assuming a reference conduit length of 1 meter):

\[ \text{KS} = \frac{\text{KH}_{\text{ring}}}{\text{RA}_{\text{m}^2}} = \frac{\text{KH}_{\text{ring}}}{\text{RA} \cdot 10^{-6}} \]

Where:

  • \(\text{KH}_{\text{ring}}\): Cumulative theoretical conductance (\(\text{m}^4\,\text{s}^{-1}\,\text{MPa}^{-1}\)).
  • RA: Analyzed ring area in \(\text{mm}^2\) (converted to \(\text{m}^2\) via \(10^{-6}\)).
  • Output unit: \(\text{m}^2\,\text{s}^{-1}\,\text{MPa}^{-1}\).

docs.title: Cell-Level Hydraulic Diameter (DH)
docs.text:
For an elliptical lumen, the hydraulic diameter is calculated following Lewis & Boose (1995):

\[ \text{DH} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \cdot a_{\mu\text{m}}^2 \cdot b_{\mu\text{m}}^2}{a_{\mu\text{m}}^2 + b_{\mu\text{m}}^2}} \]

Where \(a_{\mu\text{m}} = 2 \cdot a_{\text{semi}}\) and \(b_{\mu\text{m}} = 2 \cdot b_{\text{semi}}\) are the full major and minor axis diameters of the lumen in micrometers (\(\mu\text{m}\)).

docs.title: Ring-Level Weighted Hydraulic Diameter (DHW)
docs.text:
The conductively weighted mean hydraulic diameter per tree ring emphasizes hydraulically dominant conduits (Sperry et al. 1994; Kolb & Sperry 1999):

\[ \text{DHW} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N \text{DH}_i^5}{\sum_{i=1}^N \text{DH}_i^4} \]

docs.title: Ring-Level Mean Hydraulic Diameter (DHM)
docs.text:
The mean conduit diameter corresponding to the average Hagen-Poiseuille fourth-power conductance (Tyree & Zimmermann 2002):

\[ \text{DHM} = \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \text{DH}_i^4 \right)^{1/4} \]

docs.title: Vessel Grouping Metrics (RVGI, RVSF, RGSGV)
docs.text: In angiosperm wood, xylem vessels may appear as solitary conduits or grouped into pore multiples and clusters (Carlquist 2001).

docs.title: How Vessel Grouping Analysis Works
docs.text:
ROXAS AI identifies vessel groupings based on spatial proximity between adjacent vessel lumina:

  1. Cluster Separation Threshold: Two vessels are considered connected within the same group if the spatial separation between their lumen perimeters is less than or equal to cluster_dbl_cwt_threshold (default: 3.0 \(\mu\text{m}\), approximating intervening double cell wall thickness).
  2. Cluster Topology: Contiguous networks of connected vessels are clustered together into discrete grouping units.
  3. Topological Indices: From these clusters, standardized vessel grouping indices (Carlquist 2001) are computed:
    • Vessel Grouping Index (RVGI, ratio): Average number of vessels per grouping unit (solitary vessels count as a group of 1): \(\text{RVGI} = \frac{N_{\text{total vessels}}}{N_{\text{groups}}}\).
    • Vessel Solitary Fraction (RVSF, %): Percentage of solitary vessels relative to all vessels: \(\text{RVSF} = 100 \cdot \frac{N_{\text{solitary vessels}}}{N_{\text{total vessels}}}\).
    • Mean Group Size of Grouped Vessels (RGSGV, index): Mean number of vessels per cluster considering only non-solitary groups (\(\text{size} > 1\)).

(Note: For conifer tracheid samples, vessel grouping metrics are not applicable and are populated with blank / NA).

docs.title: Cell Wall Thickness (CWT) Quality Control & Filtering
docs.text: To obtain robust, artifact-free anatomical measurements, ROXAS AI applies automated multi-stage quality control filters to all raw cell wall thickness measurements.

docs.title: 1. Wall Definitions & Measurement Integration (Figure 1)
docs.text: Figure 1: Definition of tangential and radial wall orientations and the central measurement integration span.

docs.title: Cell Wall Identification Algorithm
docs.text:
To measure the cell wall thickness of individual cells from segmented lumen masks, ROXAS AI uses an automated Euclidean distance and watershed-based approach:

  1. Lumen Boundaries & Euclidean Distance Mask: Based on the segmented cell lumina, an inverted binary mask is created where background and cell walls are foreground pixels. A Euclidean distance transform is calculated across this mask, computing the exact spatial distance of every wall pixel to the nearest cell lumen boundary.
  2. Watershed Mask & Middle Lamella Approximation: A watershed segmentation algorithm is computed between adjacent cell lumina to detect the contact boundary (the watershed line) between neighboring tracheids. Following Prendin et al. (2017), the exact position of the middle lamella separating two adjacent cells cannot be resolved directly from optical lumen contours alone; it is therefore geometrically approximated by assuming that each wall of two adjacent sharing cells has equal thickness (i.e., the middle lamella is located equidistant between the two lumina along the watershed ridge).
  3. Lateral Integration: For each of the four anatomical wall sectors (CWTPI, CWTBA, CWTLE, CWTRI), distance values are sampled along the watershed line. To avoid geometric distortion at rounded cell corners, measurements are laterally integrated over the central portion of the wall (defined by relwidth_cwt_integration, default: 0.75 / 75%).

docs.title: Wall Sectors & Aggregated Metrics
docs.text:
For each conifer tracheid, cell walls are measured across four distinct anatomical orientations:

  • Tangential walls: CWTPI (pith-facing, top) and CWTBA (bark-facing, bottom).
  • Radial walls: CWTLE (left) and CWTRI (right).
  • Integration span: Wall thicknesses are integrated over the central span of each wall segment (defined by relwidth_cwt_integration, default: 0.75) to avoid corner-rounding biases.
  • Aggregated metrics:
    • Tangential mean: CWTTAN = (CWTPI + CWTBA) / 2; or single valid side if one is NA.
    • Radial mean: CWTRAD = (CWTLE + CWTRI) / 2; or single valid side if one is NA.
    • Overall mean: CWTALL = (CWTTAN + CWTRAD) / 2; or single valid side if one is NA.

docs.title: 2. Global IQR Distribution Filter / Tukey's Fences (Figure 2)
docs.text:
Figure 2: Global IQR outlier filtering based on lower and upper Tukey's fences.

To exclude segmentation debris, extreme clumps, or sub-pixel erosion artifacts, measurements are filtered against population-wide distributions computed independently for tangential walls (CWTPI, CWTBA) and radial walls (CWTLE, CWTRI), based on the Interquartile Range (\(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\)):

  • Lower Limit: \(\max(Q_1 - 1.5 \cdot \text{IQR},\, 1\text{ pixel in }\mu\text{m})\) (controlled by lower_limit_cwt_iqr_multiplier, default: 1.5)
  • Upper Limit: \(Q_3 + 3.0 \cdot \text{IQR}\) (controlled by upper_limit_cwt_iqr_multiplier, default: 3.0)
  • Values falling outside Lower Limit: or Upper Limit: are set to blank (NA).

docs.title: 3. Opposite Wall Ratio Filter & Percentile Exception (Figure 3)
docs.text:
Figure 3: Opposite wall ratio filter identifying and removing inflated wall measurements bordering ray cells.

In conifer xylem, opposing walls of a single tracheid have comparable thicknesses unless bordering a different anatomical structure (such as unsegmented wood ray parenchyma cells) or an intercellular gap.

  • Standard Ratio Rule: If the thickness of one wall exceeds opposite_cwt_ratio_limit \(\cdot\) opposing wall thickness (default threshold: 1.5), the larger wall is flagged for potential exclusion (NA), while the valid opposing side is retained.
  • Ray Artifacts & Wall Inflation: Wood rays run radially from pith to bark, meaning unsegmented ray contacts almost exclusively inflate radial walls (CWTLE, CWTRI, CWTRAD). Because the distance-to-watershed method assumes equal double-wall thickness between adjacent detected lumina (Prendin et al. 2017), the entire ray gap between two tracheid files is assigned as a single inflated tracheid wall. In earlywood, an unsegmented ray contact inflates thin tracheid walls (\(\sim 1.5\text{--}2.5\ \mu\text{m}\)) to \(\sim 3.5\text{--}5.0\ \mu\text{m}\) (asymmetry ratio \(\ge 1.5\text{--}2.0\times\)); in latewood, walls inflate from \(\sim 5.0\text{--}8.0\ \mu\text{m}\) to \(\ge 8.0\text{--}12.0\ \mu\text{m}\).
  • Percentile Exception Threshold (opposite_cwt_percentile_exception): To avoid falsely rejecting clean, thin earlywood walls due to benign natural ratio variations, the filter only activates when the thicker wall exceeds an empirical percentile cutoff (default: 0.60 / 60th percentile). This cutoff is calculated independently from the sample-wide distributions of tangential (CWTPI + CWTBA) and radial (CWTLE + CWTRI) walls immediately after IQR filtering. Walls thinner than the 60th percentile are protected from rejection, while walls exceeding the threshold that display opposite-side asymmetry (ratio > opposite_cwt_ratio_limit) are discarded.

docs.title: 4. Adjacent Wall Ratio Filter (Figure 4)
docs.text:
Figure 4: Adjacent wall ratio filter detecting and discarding local segmentation anomalies.

Protects against severe local segmentation anomalies (e.g., pit aperture artifacts, small pollutions, tracheids sandwiched between two rays) that disproportionately distort a single wall relative to the tracheid's perpendicular dimensions.

  • Rule: If an individual tangential wall thickness exceeds adjacent_cwt_ratio_limit \(\cdot\) perpendicular radial wall thickness (default threshold: 3.0), the distorted tangential wall is set to NA (and vice versa for radial walls).

docs.title: 5. CWT Quality Assurance Layer & File Lifecycle
docs.text:
To support visual validation and interactive quality control of cell wall thickness measurements, ROXAS AI includes a dedicated CWT QA layer and data export workflow:

  • Data File (<sample>.cwt.json): During measurement (Widget 9A or 9B), measurement circle coordinates, wall thickness values, sector orientations, inclusion/exclusion status, and specific filter exclusion reasons are serialized directly to disk in <sample>.cwt.json.
  • Napari QA Layer ([<sample>] CWT Circles): Rendered directly in the viewer on sampled cells (default: every 25th cell, configured via cwt_visualization.sample_interval). Circles are color-coded (green/lime for included, red for excluded).
  • Interactive Tooltips: Hovering the cursor over any measurement circle displays a tooltip with Cell ID, Sector (Pith/Bark/Left/Right), Thickness (\(\mu\text{m}\)), Status (included/excluded), and descriptive Exclusion Reason.
  • Automatic Loading: When loading a sample in Widget 2/4, if <sample>.cwt.json exists and cwt_visualization.enabled is true, the [<sample>] CWT Circles layer is automatically loaded and displayed.
  • Mutual Editor Exclusion: During manual cell editing (Widget 5) and ring editing (Widget 6), [<sample>] CWT Circles is automatically hidden to eliminate visual clutter and prevent accidental cross-layer edits, and restored when exiting edit mode.
  • Synchronization: Re-running measurements in Widget 9A or 9B automatically recalculates and overwrites <sample>.cwt.json and refreshes the QA layer in napari.

docs.title: Mork's Index (RTSR) and Circular Ratio (CTSR, Figure 5)
docs.text:
Mork's index distinguishes earlywood from latewood tracheids based on the ratio between tangential cell wall thickness and radial lumen diameter (Denne 1989):

Figure 5: Definition of Mork's index based on tangential cell wall thickness and radial lumen diameter.

Mathematically, Mork's radial thickness-to-span ratio (RTSR) is defined as:

\[ \text{RTSR} = \frac{4 \cdot \text{CWTTAN}}{\text{DRAD}} = \frac{2 \cdot (\text{CWTPI} + \text{CWTBA})}{\text{DRAD}} \]

A conifer tracheid is classified as latewood when RTSR \(\ge 1\) (i.e., when twice the double tangential cell wall thickness equals or exceeds the radial lumen diameter).

Similarly, the circular thickness-to-span ratio (CTSR) relates overall wall thickness to the diameter of an area-equivalent circle (\(d_{\text{circ}} = 2\sqrt{\text{LA}/\pi}\)):

\[ \text{CTSR} = \frac{4 \cdot \text{CWTALL}}{2\sqrt{\text{LA} / \pi}} \]

docs.title: Cell Wall Reinforcement Index (TB2, Figure 6)
docs.text:
The cell wall reinforcement index estimates conduit resistance against cell wall collapse (implosion) induced by negative xylem pressure (Hacke et al. 2001):

Figure 6: Definition of the cell wall reinforcement index \((t/b)^2\).

The index evaluates the double wall thickness (\(t = 2 \cdot \text{CWT}\)) relative to the internal lumen span (\(b = \text{Diameter}\)) independently for radial and tangential orientations:

\[ (t/b)_{\text{rad}}^2 = \left( \frac{2 \cdot \text{CWTRAD}}{\text{DRAD}} \right)^2 = \left( \frac{\text{CWTLE} + \text{CWTRI}}{\text{DRAD}} \right)^2 \] \[ (t/b)_{\text{tan}}^2 = \left( \frac{2 \cdot \text{CWTTAN}}{\text{DTAN}} \right)^2 = \left( \frac{\text{CWTPI} + \text{CWTBA}}{\text{DTAN}} \right)^2 \]

Because mechanical buckling occurs along the weaker orientation, the final index is taken as the minimum:

\[ \text{TB2} = \min\left( (t/b)_{\text{rad}}^2, \, (t/b)_{\text{tan}}^2 \right) \]

docs.title: Relative Anatomical Density (RWD) and Cell Wall Area (CWA)
docs.text:
Cell wall area (CWA) and relative anatomical density (RWD) quantify the proportion of wood volume occupied by cell wall material:

  • Cell Wall Area (CWA, \(\mu\text{m}^2\)): Area of the cell wall envelope surrounding the lumen: \(\text{CWA} = \text{CA} - \text{LA}\), where CA is total cross-sectional cell area (lumen plus cell wall) and LA is lumen area. CWA is computed only when all four base wall measurements (CWTPI, CWTBA, CWTLE, CWTRI) are valid and CA > LA.
  • Relative Anatomical Density (RWD, ratio \([0, 1]\)): Fractional cell wall volume: \(\text{RWD} = \frac{\text{CWA}}{\text{CA}} = \frac{\text{CWA}}{\text{CWA} + \text{LA}}\).

docs.title: Relative Radial Position in Ring (RRADDISTR)
docs.text:
RRADDISTR defines the relative positioning of each cell along the radial formation trajectory within its annual growth ring:

\[ \text{RRADDISTR} = 100 \cdot \frac{d_{\text{top}}}{d_{\text{top}} + d_{\text{bot}}} \]

Where:

  • \(d_{\text{top}}\) (RADDISTR): Distance (\(\mu\text{m}\)) from the proximal (pith-side / upper) ring boundary to the cell centroid along the local radial trajectory.
  • \(d_{\text{bot}}\): Distance (\(\mu\text{m}\)) from the cell centroid to the distal (bark-side / lower) ring boundary along the local radial trajectory.
  • Local ring width is the total distance between proximal and distal boundaries passing through the cell centroid along the radial trajectory (\(d_{\text{top}} + d_{\text{bot}}\)).
  • Values range from \(0.00\%\) (cell centered directly on the proximal ring boundary) to \(100.00\%\) (cell centered on the distal ring boundary).

docs.title: Accounting for Ring Boundary Inclination
docs.text:
In wood cross-sections, annual ring boundaries are rarely strictly horizontal. ROXAS AI accounts for boundary inclination:

  1. Vertical Distances: First, the vertical distances along the pixel column of the cell centroid from the proximal (\(d_{\text{top, vert}}\)) and distal (\(d_{\text{bot, vert}}\)) ring boundaries are determined from the rasterized ring boundary polygons.
  2. Handling Differing Boundary Inclination Angles: If the proximal (top) boundary and distal (bottom) boundary have different inclination angles (\(\theta_{\text{top}}\) and \(\theta_{\text{bot}}\)), ROXAS AI calculates the mean inclination angle for the cell: \(\theta_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\theta_{\text{top}} + \theta_{\text{bot}}}{2}\).
  3. Angled Distance Correction: The radial distances orthogonal to the local ring orientation are then obtained by projecting the vertical distances along the mean inclination: \(d_{\text{top}} = d_{\text{top, vert}} \cdot \cos(\theta_{\text{avg}})\) and \(d_{\text{bot}} = d_{\text{bot, vert}} \cdot \cos(\theta_{\text{avg}})\). This ensures that both absolute radial distance (RADDISTR = \(d_{\text{top}}\)) and relative radial position (RRADDISTR) remain geometrically accurate even across tapered, wedging, or non-parallel tree rings.

docs.title: The Metadata File (.metadata.json)
docs.text: The metadata file ensures traceability and reproducibility of your analysis. It stores four main categories of information:

docs.title: 1. Sample & Project Information
docs.text:
• sample_name: The unique identifier for the wood sample.
  • sample_stem_path: The relative path of the sample within the project directory.
  • sample_type: The type of wood (i.e., conifer or angiosperm; note that the angiosperm analysis is not implemented yet).
  • meas_geometry: The measurement layout (i.e., linear or circular; note that the circular analysis is not implemented yet).
  • rings_outmost_complete_year: The calendar year assigned to the most recent complete tree ring.
  • reference_series: The cross-dating reference series used (or NA if none).

docs.title: 2. Imaging & Spatial Metadata
docs.text:
• spatial_resolution: The conversion factor from pixels to micrometers (\(\text{px}/\mu\text{m}\)). This is critical for all subsequent physical measurements.
  • scan_size: The dimensions of the original image in pixels (Height, Width).
  • scan_info: Detailed technical info about the image, including the detected DPI (Dots Per Inch).
  • scan_exif: Metadata extracted directly from the image file (e.g., software used for scanning, capture date).

docs.title: 3. Processing & Traceability
docs.text:
• sw_version: The exact version of ROXAS AI used for the analysis.
  • meas_by: The username or system identifier that ran the measurement analysis.
  • cells_segmentation_model & rings_segmentation_model: The specific AI model filenames (.pth / .pt) used for detection.
  • meas_created_at: A timestamp of when the final measurement table was generated.

docs.title: 4. Analysis Parameters & Quality Control
docs.text:
These parameters define how cell walls are measured and how clusters are handled:

  • cluster_dbl_cwt_threshold: Distance threshold in \(\mu\text{m}\) for detecting vessel groupings in angiosperms (see Vessel Grouping Metrics).
  • relwidth_cwt_integration: Relative wall fraction along the cell wall used for thickness integration (see Wall Definitions & Measurement Integration).
  • lower_limit_cwt_iqr_multiplier: Multiplier for the lower Tukey's fence (\(Q_1 - k \cdot \text{IQR}\)) in cell wall thickness outlier detection (see Global IQR Distribution Filter).
  • upper_limit_cwt_iqr_multiplier: Multiplier for the upper Tukey's fence (\(Q_3 + k \cdot \text{IQR}\)) in cell wall thickness outlier detection (see Global IQR Distribution Filter).
  • opposite_cwt_ratio_limit: Maximum allowed ratio between opposite wall thicknesses before triggering exclusion (see Opposite Wall Ratio Filter & Percentile Exception).
  • opposite_cwt_percentile_exception: Directional quantile cutoff (default: 0.60 / 60%) above which opposite-wall ratio filtering applies, protecting thin earlywood walls from false rejection while capturing ray artifacts (see Opposite Wall Ratio Filter & Percentile Exception).
  • adjacent_cwt_ratio_limit: Maximum allowed ratio between adjacent wall thicknesses (see Adjacent Wall Ratio Filter).

docs.title: Global Settings (settings.json)
docs.text:
While the .metadata.json is unique to each sample, the settings.json file stores your global preferences and plugin configurations.

Important: One of the core goals of ROXAS AI is to be accessible. Unlike classical systems, no expert knowledge is required to configure these settings. For most users, the default values are optimized for professional results and do not need to be changed.

The settings are organized into several logical blocks:

docs.title: 1. File Extensions (file_extensions)
docs.text:
Defines how ROXAS AI recognizes and names files:

  • scan_file_extension: File suffix for prepared scan images. (Default: [".scan", ".jpg"])
  • cells_file_extension: File suffix for cell segmentation label masks. (Default: [".cells", ".png"])
  • cells_table_file_extension: File suffix for cell-level measurement tables. (Default: [".cells_table", ".csv"])
  • rings_file_extension: File suffix for ring boundary label masks. (Default: [".rings", ".tif"])
  • rings_table_file_extension: File suffix for ring-level measurement tables. (Default: [".rings_table", ".csv"])
  • metadata_file_extension: File suffix for sample metadata JSON files. (Default: [".metadata", ".json"])
  • crossdating_file_extension: File suffix for Tucson cross-dating files. (Default: [".crossdating", ".txt"])
  • cwt_file_extension: File suffix for CWT QA datasets. (Default: [".cwt", ".json"])
  • roxas_file_extensions: List of managed ROXAS file suffixes. (Default: [".scan", ".cells", ".rings", ".metadata", ".cwt"])
  • image_file_extensions: Supported image formats. (Default: [".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".tif", ".tiff", ".bmp", ".jp2"])
  • text_file_extensions: Supported text and table formats. (Default: [".rwl", ".tuc", ".txt", ".csv", ".tsv"])

docs.title: 2. Processing & GPU (processing)
docs.text:
Allows configuring hardware acceleration and memory optimization:

  • try_to_use_gpu: Set to true to enable GPU acceleration if a compatible CUDA-enabled graphics card, Apple Silicon (MPS), or Intel GPU (XPU) is available. (Default: false)
  • try_to_use_autocast: Set to true for mixed precision acceleration during deep learning inference. (Default: false)

docs.title: 3. Tables (tables)
docs.text:
Defines the output format for tabular data:

  • separator: Column delimiter for output tables. (Default: ";")
  • index_column: Column identifier name. (Default: "id")

docs.title: 4. Visualization (Vectorization & Rasterization)
docs.text: Controls geometric conversion algorithms, contour simplification tolerances, layer styling, and colormaps in the napari viewer:

docs.title: Vectorization Parameters (vectorization)
docs.text:
Controls how raster label masks are converted into editable vector polygons and polylines:

  • cells_tolerance: Maximum geometric approximation tolerance in pixels for Douglas-Peucker cell contour simplification. Eliminates single-pixel staircase artefacts while preserving lumen fidelity. (Default: 1)
  • cells_edge_width: Display line width (in pixels) of cell vector boundaries in the viewer. (Default: 5)
  • cells_edge_color: Outline color for cell vector shapes. (Default: "blue")
  • cells_face_color: Fill color for cell vector shapes. (Default: "cyan")
  • rings_tolerance: Maximum approximation tolerance in pixels for Douglas-Peucker ring polyline smoothing. Set to 0 to disable simplification and retain raw pixel coordinates. (Default: 5)
  • rings_edge_width: Display line thickness (in pixels) for ring boundary polylines. (Default: 7)
  • rings_edge_color: Display color for active ring boundary polylines. (Default: "black")
  • rerun_interactive_edge_color: Display color for newly detected boundaries generated during interactive AI re-runs. (Default: "lime")

docs.title: Rasterization & Colormaps (rasterization)
docs.text:
Controls how edited vector shapes are rasterized back onto integer label masks:

  • cells_color: Default colormap color for rasterized cell lumens. (Default: "lime")
  • uncomplete_ring_value: Integer label assigned to the topmost uncompleted ring zone bordering the bark edge. (Default: -1)
  • uncomplete_ring_color: Display color assigned to the uncompleted ring zone. (Default: "red")
  • rings_color_sequence: List of alternating colors assigned cyclically to successive annual rings. (Default: ["blue", "green", "yellow", "purple", "orange", "cyan", "brown", "pink", "gray", "lime"])

docs.title: 5. CWT Quality Assurance & Visualization (cwt_visualization)
docs.text:
Configures the interactive cell wall thickness visualization layer rendered in napari (see CWT Quality Assurance Layer & File Lifecycle for full details):

  • enabled: Toggle creation and display of the [<sample>] CWT Circles Shapes layer. (Default: true)
  • sample_interval: Step stride for cell sampling along the cross-section (e.g., displaying circles on every 25th tracheid). (Default: 25)
  • included_color: Outline color for valid, measurement-included wall sectors. (Default: "lime")
  • excluded_color: Outline color for filtered/excluded wall sectors. (Default: "red")
  • edge_width: Line thickness (in pixels) for measurement circles. (Default: 3.0)

docs.title: 6. Measurement Defaults (measurements)
docs.text:
Contains default parameters for anatomical analysis, used to populate metadata for new samples:

  • cluster_dbl_cwt_threshold: Distance threshold in \(\mu\text{m}\) for detecting vessel groupings in angiosperms (see Vessel Grouping Metrics). (Default: 3.0)
  • cells_smoothing_kernel_size: Size of the kernel used for smoothing cell boundaries (see Cell Wall Identification Algorithm). (Default: 1)
  • relwidth_cwt_integration: Relative wall fraction along the cell wall used for thickness integration (see Wall Definitions & Measurement Integration). (Default: 0.75)
  • cells_tangential_angle: Default sample orientation angle in degrees clockwise. (Default: 0.0)
  • lower_limit_cwt_iqr_multiplier: Multiplier for the lower Tukey's fence in CWT outlier detection (see Global IQR Distribution Filter). (Default: 1.5)
  • upper_limit_cwt_iqr_multiplier: Multiplier for the upper Tukey's fence in CWT outlier detection (see Global IQR Distribution Filter). (Default: 3.0)
  • opposite_cwt_ratio_limit: Maximum allowed ratio between opposite wall thicknesses before filtering (see Opposite Wall Ratio Filter & Percentile Exception). (Default: 1.5)
  • opposite_cwt_percentile_exception: Directional quantile cutoff exempting thin earlywood walls from opposite-wall ratio filtering (see Opposite Wall Ratio Filter & Percentile Exception). (Default: 0.60)
  • adjacent_cwt_ratio_limit: Maximum allowed ratio between adjacent wall thicknesses (see Adjacent Wall Ratio Filter). (Default: 3.0)

docs.title: 7. Annotated Image & Project Directory
docs.text:
• project_directory: Path to the currently active project working directory. (Default: null)
  • annotated_image: Configuration for saved annotated verification images (_annotated.jpg):
    • cell_opacity: Opacity percentage (0–100) of the cell overlay. (Default: 50)
    • cell_fill_color: Fill color for cell lumina. (Default: "yellow")
    • year_label_size: Calendar year label font size as percentage of mean ring width. (Default: 20)
    • scale_factor: Scale factor for image downscaling (1.0 = original dimensions). (Default: 1.0)
    • quality: JPEG quality rating (1–100). (Default: 75)

docs.title: 8. Metadata Field Definitions (samples_metadata)
docs.text:
Defines the structure, validation rules, and widget types for the input forms in the plugin:

  • sample_name: Text input for the unique sample identifier. (Read-only)
  • sample_type: Dropdown selection for wood type (conifer, angiosperm). (Default: "conifer")
  • meas_geometry: Dropdown selection for measurement layout (linear, circular). (Default: "linear")
  • spatial_resolution: Numeric input for spatial resolution in \(\text{px}/\mu\text{m}\). (Default: 2.267574)
  • rings_outmost_complete_year: Integer input for the calendar year of the outermost complete ring. (Default: 9999 / "Not set")
